sections.title: A rooftop array is a chain of interfaces
paragraphs: The module rectangle is the visible part of a rooftop system. Its support begins at an approved interface on the module frame, continues through clamps or direct attachments into rails or other members, and then through the roof attachment into the building. Each link must resist the forces passed to it. A strong rail cannot compensate for an attachment that misses its intended structural member, and a well-fastened attachment cannot rescue a module supported outside its approved zones.

Begin a review by drawing this chain and naming the exact products at each interface. Distinguish what is known from what merely looks plausible in a layout. A roof photograph can establish visible obstructions and covering type, but hidden decking condition, rafter dimensions and previous alterations require other evidence. The goal of early planning is a coherent proposal that an installer and structural reviewer can assess.

sections.title: Gravity is only one loading direction
paragraphs: Modules and mounting hardware add permanent weight. Snow can add variable downward loading, while wind can create uplift and horizontal forces. Those forces depend on the building, surrounding exposure, roof geometry and array location. Roof-edge and corner regions may need different treatment from the interior. Counting panel mass therefore answers only a small part of the structural question.

A useful beginner habit is to separate demand from capacity. Demand is the force the design must accommodate under its governing combinations; capacity is what the specified assembly can support under its evaluated conditions. A module's published mechanical test value is not automatically the allowable load of the complete roof installation. Ask the designer which adopted building-code edition and site inputs govern the project, rather than copying a load table from another address.

sections.title: Water needs a continuous route
paragraphs: A roof works as a layered water-management system. Adding a penetration changes that system locally, so flashing, seals and their relationship to the covering must follow the selected roof and mounting details. A visible bead of sealant is not evidence that water entering upslope will drain correctly. Conversely, a nonpenetrating clamp on a metal seam still requires a compatible seam and a roof that can transfer the load.

Record covering material, installation age, previous leaks and proposed roof replacement. Discuss sequencing with the roofer: installing an array shortly before replacement can add removal, storage and reinstallation costs. Clarify responsibility for roof damage and workmanship, including who attends if a leak is reported after commissioning. The useful deliverable is a documented interface and service responsibility, not a generic promise that all solar mounts are waterproof.

sections.title: Module fit and mounting compatibility are separate
paragraphs: The IronRidge XR manual illustrates why product combinations matter: its compatibility, attachment and bonding provisions belong to a specific evaluated system. Use the manual revision applicable to the purchased parts, together with the module installation instructions. Frame depth, clamp engagement, permissible support location, rail span, splice position and cantilever are related decisions. Changing module format late in procurement can change more than the wattage.

For standing-seam metal, S-5!'s clamp-to-seam tool organizes tested combinations by actual roof profile and other identifying details. A name such as standing seam does not specify one universal clamp. Trace the load beyond the seam into roof panels, clips and supporting members. Before ordering, request a parts schedule that identifies the full assembly and marks substitutions requiring renewed review.

sections.title: Reserve access before filling the roof
paragraphs: Draw skylights, vents, roof hatches, drains, equipment and locally required access areas before arranging modules. Distinguish fire-service access, installer work space and future maintenance access; they can overlap but have different reasons. A convenient route for carrying equipment must also form part of a planned safe work method. OSHA's US solar fall-hazard guidance highlights roof edges, skylights and lifting panels as specific concerns, and distinguishes installation from maintenance requirements.

For a planning model, use exclusions whose dimensions and reasons are recorded. Do not present a universal setback number as a code rule for every jurisdiction. Confirm requirements with the authority having jurisdiction and the project designer. A layout that preserves access may use fewer modules but make inspection, repair and roof maintenance practicable. These provisions belong in the first drawing, because they are expensive to recover after the roof is filled.

sections.title: Worked example: weight describes one question

workedExample.title: Twelve hypothetical modules on a usable roof plane
givens: 12 modules, each 23 kg and 2.0 m².
Mounting assembly mass assumed 48 kg total.
Ignore snow, wind, seismic forces and the roof's own existing loads; this is only mass bookkeeping.
steps: Module mass is 12 × 23 = 276 kg; total added mass is 276 + 48 = 324 kg.
Module surface area is 12 × 2.0 = 24 m².
An average over that module area is 324 ÷ 24 = 13.5 kg/m², equivalent to about 0.132 kN/m² under standard gravity.
Record the result as an average added permanent load estimate, then ask the designer to resolve attachment reactions and all other governing loads.
workedExample.result: The estimate is 324 kg total, not a structural approval.
workedExample.discussion: The weight is carried at discrete support points. Dividing by area does not establish local roof capacity or predict wind uplift. A broader roof-area average would produce a smaller number without reducing the actual attachment forces.

sections.title: A reviewable roof record
paragraphs: Organize the proposal around evidence that remains useful after installation. A future technician should be able to identify a mount, module and roof detail without reconstructing the design from sales emails. Keep drawing revisions tied to the actual bill of materials and record any site change that affects an interface.
rows: What was installed beneath the modules

sections.title: Mistakes that create false confidence
paragraphs: A polished three-dimensional view can hide every important roof interface. Treat its clean appearance as communication quality rather than structural evidence. Likewise, a permit application that names a mounting family but omits the actual attachment leaves a material question unresolved. Ask for the drawing and calculation package associated with the selected configuration.

Avoid distributing a total load equally over an arbitrary number of mounts to choose attachment spacing. Real reactions depend on the support arrangement and loading. Avoid mixing torque values between hardware generations or treating every bonding device as reusable. When parts change, ask which documentation changes with them. This is also why a photographic completion record should include hidden interfaces before modules obscure them.

sections.title: Exercise: identical arrays, different evidence

exercise.question: Two houses fit the same twelve-module layout. One has asphalt shingles and rafters; the other has standing-seam metal. Can the first house's attachment detail approve the second?
exercise.answer: No. The geometric pattern can be reused as a starting point, but the roof attachment and load path must be verified for each building.
exercise.explanation: The covering, structural interfaces, tested hardware combinations and site demands differ. Reusing the pattern is a layout decision; reusing an unsupported attachment detail would skip the evidence needed to establish compatibility.

paragraphs: Before proceeding, summarize the covering and condition, identify the intended attachment family, and list the open structural and access questions. These are the inputs that turn a roof sketch into a useful installation discussion.

sections.title: Ground mounting exchanges one constraint for several others
paragraphs: A ground array avoids placing modules on a building roof, but it occupies land and introduces foundation, access and trenching questions. Start with a site plan that includes boundaries, buildings, vegetation, drainage, slopes and the route to the electrical equipment. Mark uncertainty about buried services before deciding where posts or trenches belong. The clean rectangular area visible in a satellite image may contain easements, seasonal wet ground or future uses that make it unsuitable.

Separate the project into layout, structure and electrical route. Layout asks where modules and access fit. Structure asks how forces reach suitable ground. The route asks how energy reaches conversion equipment without incompatible distances or installation conditions. Solving one does not solve the others. Early comparison should preserve multiple locations long enough to understand the trade between sunlight, foundation practicality and total installed cost.

figures.caption: Level-ground row geometry: footprint, gap and pitch are distinct quantities. This sketch is not a foundation design.
figures.alt: Two tilted rows show panel rise, horizontal footprint, open gap and complete row pitch.

sections.title: Define the three spacing quantities
paragraphs: A tilted row has a horizontal projection called its footprint. The open distance from the back of one footprint to the front of the next is the clear gap. Row pitch is measured between equivalent points on adjacent rows and includes both footprint and gap. If a tool labels a slider spacing, find out which quantity it changes before comparing its result with another drawing.

For a table of modules, use the entire sloped table length in the relevant cross-section rather than one module's dimension. Two stacked modules at the same tilt approximately double that length, before accounting for their gap. The low-edge clearance above ground is another quantity. Equal clearances in neighboring rows cancel in the simplest shadow construction; unequal clearances or sloping terrain require a different geometry. Label all of these inputs rather than allowing a pleasing visual scale to imply measurements.

sections.title: A shadow picture is a geometric observation
paragraphs: Low sun elevation makes a longer shadow from a given height. Solar azimuth determines where that shadow falls in plan view. An aligned cross-section describes the special case when the sun points perpendicular to the row; it does not capture every morning and afternoon. Terrain and external obstructions complicate both the length and direction of shadows.

A single date and time can show a design problem, but an unshaded view cannot establish all-year performance. Annual energy modeling combines many operating conditions, irradiance, temperatures and electrical behavior. Sandia's PV performance modeling resources provide a framework for keeping geometry and energy calculations distinct. If a preview does not calculate energy, describe its output as a shade visualization. Do not translate a shaded surface percentage directly into the same percentage of energy loss without an appropriate electrical and time-series model.

sections.title: Choose a shading objective before optimizing panel count
paragraphs: There is no single row spacing that is best for every project. A spacious layout may reduce winter self-shading while using more land and wiring; a denser one may increase total generation per site despite some shade. A household that values winter backup may rank those layouts differently from a project seeking maximum annual generation. Establish the success measure first.

Compare alternatives using the same weather data, terrain assumptions, module configuration and loss model. Include usable land, total module count and the annual or seasonal energy outcome. Explain any assumed solar-position window used for a geometric screening rule. A rule based on winter noon should be labeled winter-noon screening, not all-day no shading. Keep room for vegetation management and equipment access in both alternatives so a dense energy model does not hide an impractical site.

sections.title: Foundations need soil evidence
paragraphs: Posts may be supported by concrete, driven foundations or an approved ground-screw arrangement. Suitability depends on actual ground conditions and loading rather than the general attractiveness of a foundation type. Soil variability, rock, corrosion exposure, frost and groundwater can affect the solution. Request the evidence required by the foundation designer and manufacturer, including any testing and acceptance criteria.

IronRidge's ground-screw guidance separates screw-manufacturer installation instructions from assembly of the supported array. Its ground-mount system documentation describes a specific racking family; it does not authorize arbitrary foundation substitution. A screw that installs easily is not thereby proven adequate for pullout or lateral demands. Record rejected locations and test results alongside accepted ones, because moving a post to avoid an obstruction can also change the structural arrangement.

sections.title: Worked example: a level-ground screening calculation

workedExample.title: A 2 m sloped table at 30°
givens: Table length in the north–south cross-section: 2.00 m.
Tilt: 30°; design screening sun elevation: 20°.
Level ground, equal low-edge height, rows aligned with the sun's cross-section; ignore external shade and finite-width effects.
steps: Horizontal footprint = 2.00 × cos(30°) = 1.73 m.
Clear gap for this instant = 1.00 ÷ tan(20°) = 2.75 m.
Pitch = footprint + gap = 1.73 + 2.75 = 4.48 m.
Label the drawing with this date/time geometry and send denser and wider alternatives for energy modeling.
workedExample.result: About 4.48 m pitch avoids the modeled row shadow at the assumed aligned 20° sun elevation.
workedExample.discussion: It does not guarantee all-day winter clearance, a particular annual yield, or a valid foundation. A lower sun angle increases the calculated gap; a two-module-high table changes the rise and footprint.

sections.title: Compare complete site alternatives
paragraphs: A site-selection table should identify the source of each estimate and leave genuinely unknown values visible. A shorter cable route can be valuable, but it should not erase severe shade or drainage difficulties. Keep capital cost and operating burden in the same comparison.
rows: Affects installed cost and electrical design

sections.title: Common mistakes and practical ownership
paragraphs: Measuring pitch from an aerial view while entering gap into a calculator creates an inconsistent comparison. So does evaluating one alternative with mature trees and another with no vegetation. Use dimensions that can be checked on site and distinguish existing conditions from proposed changes.

Plan how a technician reaches every row without walking on modules or damaging conductors. Consider mowers, grazing animals or other site activity only when their interaction with cables and equipment is resolved. A perimeter fence or landscape plan may change access and shade. Do not assume a ground array is inherently easy to maintain: its wiring remains electrical equipment, and wind damage, erosion or vegetation can require qualified inspection. Record the final row map and underground route as part of the owner handover.

sections.title: Exercise: what changed when tilt increased?

exercise.question: A table remains 2 m long but its tilt rises from 30° to 45°. At the same aligned 20° sun elevation, does its smaller horizontal footprint guarantee a smaller row pitch?
exercise.answer: No. Its rise increases enough to lengthen the required shadow gap.
exercise.explanation: At 45°, footprint and rise are each about 1.414 m. The gap is 1.414 ÷ tan(20°) ≈ 3.89 m, so pitch is approximately 5.30 m. Tilt improves some light-capture conditions while changing land use; it must be compared through the full objective.

paragraphs: Keep the screening calculation with the assumptions, then compare the resulting layouts through the site, structure and electrical questions. An explicit uncertainty is more useful than an unexplained recommended spacing.

sections.title: Survey the questions as well as the roof
paragraphs: A useful roof survey connects a proposed array to a real building. It captures dimensions, orientation, pitch, covering, obstructions, shade and the evidence needed to review structure. It also records information that cannot be established safely or reliably from the available view. An unverified measurement should stay marked as unverified rather than becoming a precise-looking number in a drawing.

Plan the survey around decisions. Module fit needs usable dimensions. Annual production needs orientation and shade. Mounting needs the roof interface and structural arrangement. Roof replacement planning needs condition and remaining-life information. The survey does not have to answer every engineering question itself, but it must make those questions visible and assign them to someone able to resolve them. This approach helps avoid ordering a module format that only fits in an inaccurate aerial image.

figures.caption: The roof survey must describe visible covering and the hidden structural interfaces behind it. This conceptual section is not a roof-access plan.
figures.alt: Solar mounting components are shown over a roof covering and supporting building structure.

sections.title: Dimensions need a datum and a method
paragraphs: Choose a consistent reference corner or line for each roof plane. Record overall usable dimensions and the position of every obstruction relative to that datum. Give the measurement method and realistic uncertainty. A satellite image, laser measurement, construction drawing and physical survey can disagree for understandable reasons; identify which controls each quantity.

Distinguish sloped roof distance from horizontal projection. A roof plane with horizontal run R and pitch angle θ has sloped distance R ÷ cos θ in that direction. Confusing those distances can either understate or overstate usable space depending on what the layout expects. Label units and whether dimensions describe a horizontal plan or the roof surface. An apparently generous fit with only a few centimeters spare deserves explicit field confirmation before equipment is purchased.

sections.title: Roof condition changes the installation sequence
paragraphs: Record covering type, approximate age, known repairs, leaks and evidence of deterioration. Include gutters, drains, flashing, valleys and previous penetrations because the array must coexist with their water-management role. The owner may know recurring problems that a single dry-weather visit cannot reveal. Ask the roofer to assess matters outside the surveyor's expertise.

If the roof will need replacement during the planned ownership period, compare replacement before installation with later module removal and reinstallation. Keep reroofing cost, solar work cost and lost production distinct. A longer module performance warranty does not extend the life of the roof beneath it. Document the roof warranty's requirements for attachments and who retains responsibility for the weatherproofing interface after construction. These decisions can change the project more than a small gain in rated module watts.

sections.title: Structure is more than finding rafters
paragraphs: Roof attachments need an approved load path, but confirming where a rafter appears is only the beginning. Supporting-member size, span, spacing, condition and alterations can affect review. Roof coverings or access limitations may hide these features. Construction drawings may be outdated, so distinguish original drawings from observed conditions.

Prepare a structural evidence list for the qualified reviewer rather than choosing attachment spacing from a photograph. Include proposed module dimensions and mass, mounting family and array location. Site wind, snow and other governing loads must be assessed using the locally adopted requirements. If the reviewer requests further investigation, update the evidence pack and revision history. A plausible rail span from a manufacturer's table cannot establish the capacity of the existing roof structure by itself.

sections.title: Shade requires time and direction
paragraphs: Record roof-plane azimuth and tilt, and identify nearby trees, buildings, chimneys and parapets that can block sunlight. Distinguish permanent objects from proposed vegetation management or future development. An obstruction may shade the array only in a particular season or time window, so photographs should include date, time and viewpoint.

A shade survey should support the energy model's inputs. Explain whether the estimate comes from measured horizon data, a documented model or a simple visual screen. The location of one shadow does not directly quantify annual loss. Electrical mismatch and module configuration can change the effect of partial shade, while microinverters or optimizers cannot recover sunlight that never reaches the cells. Keep the loss-model assumptions with the shade record so later equipment changes can be reviewed consistently.

sections.title: Worked example: a fit that needs field confirmation

workedExample.title: Eight modules across a fictional roof plane
givens: Usable width estimated from an aerial image: 9.20 m, uncertainty ±0.15 m.
Eight modules each 1.10 m wide; seven intermodule gaps assumed 0.02 m.
The usable width already excludes all proposed access and obstruction zones; no edge clearance is being prescribed.
steps: Nominal occupied width = 8 × 1.10 + 7 × 0.02 = 8.94 m.
Nominal spare width = 9.20 − 8.94 = 0.26 m.
At the lower estimate, spare width is 9.05 − 8.94 = 0.11 m.
Check the selected mounting tolerances and confirmed exclusion dimensions before treating the eight-column arrangement as buildable.
workedExample.result: The drawing suggests eight modules may fit, but the 0.26 m nominal margin is comparable with survey uncertainty.
workedExample.discussion: A better measurement can settle the issue. Reducing nominal gaps below approved values to rescue a layout changes the assembly rather than improving the survey.

sections.title: Access and routing belong in the survey
paragraphs: Identify installer access, safe lifting arrangements, future maintenance routes and applicable fire-service pathways. OSHA's US guidance identifies skylights and roof edges as fall hazards; a building feature visible in a photograph should not be assumed safe to stand on. A qualified site team chooses the actual protection and access method.

Also sketch the cable and equipment route. Show where wiring leaves the roof and where conversion or storage equipment could be located. Check that proposed locations preserve manufacturer clearances and owner access. A distant convenient wall can change wiring design and cost; an attic location can create temperature and serviceability questions. Keep this route conceptual until the electrical designer resolves its installation conditions.

sections.title: The roof evidence pack
paragraphs: Label drawing versions so a contractor can tell whether a module swap, roof repair or new obstruction was incorporated. Preserve original survey evidence separately from the final proposed layout. A record of how the layout was derived makes future reconfiguration much easier than a lone polished rendering.

sections.title: Mistakes and an explained exercise
paragraphs: Avoid recording spurious precision, assuming every roof plane faces the same direction, or measuring an obstruction's center while ignoring its footprint. Do not count a required pathway as spare space when calculating maximum module quantity. A roof survey is complete when its evidence and open questions are usable, not when every cell in a spreadsheet contains a number.

exercise.question: A layout says twelve modules fit because the roof measures 30 m² and the modules total 24 m². What evidence is missing?
exercise.answer: The actual dimensioned arrangement and exclusions, plus mounting, structural and access evidence.
exercise.explanation: Area alone ignores rectangular packing, setbacks, obstructions and support zones. Two roofs with equal area can have very different usable shapes. A fit claim needs measured dimensions and a specific layout before the separate approval questions are considered.

sections.title: A mounting family is a design approach
paragraphs: Rail-based, rail-less and direct-to-metal-roof systems describe how modules are supported, not a universal approval for a roof. Begin with the covering and supporting building, then examine the manufacturer's documented assembly. The most useful comparison asks what connects to what, what can be adjusted, and which conditions the evidence covers.

A rail-based system bridges roof attachments with members that support module clamps. A rail-less approach locates modules through shorter or direct support components. A standing-seam arrangement may use approved seam clamps with rails or approved direct module interfaces. These descriptions help organize questions, but the actual product still controls compatible frame dimensions, fasteners, bonding devices and support locations. A shorter parts list can reduce some work while placing tighter demands on roof geometry or module positioning.

figures.caption: Compare families by following each interface. Some systems omit a long rail but still require a verified load path.
figures.alt: Module support transfers through mounting hardware into the roof and supporting members.

sections.title: Rails provide alignment, within limits
paragraphs: Rails can offer practical alignment and attachment flexibility. Their span, cantilever, splice placement and thermal movement provisions still impose limits. A long member is not an invitation to place attachments wherever they are convenient. Different rail profiles may be suitable for different load conditions, and their appearance alone does not establish interchangeable capacity.

Ask how an installer will preserve module support zones while locating roof attachments. The module manual and racking manual must agree at that interface. Record permitted orientations and the exact clamp family. IronRidge's XR manual version 5.2 is one example of documentation that separates compatibility, hardware and assembly provisions. This chapter does not carry its torque or span values into unrelated systems; values belong to the exact parts and applicable design package.

sections.title: Rail-less systems move the coordination problem
paragraphs: Removing long rails changes logistics and alignment, but it does not remove structural or bonding requirements. A roof-plane irregularity that a rail system accommodates through approved adjustments may require another solution in a direct support system. Assess how the selected product deals with uneven surfaces, module gaps, frame tolerances and cable support.

A useful quotation should identify the product's actual installation details and the module compatibility evidence. Compare labor assumptions and future module replacement, not just kilograms of aluminum. Ask whether removing one module disturbs neighboring modules or a bonding path, and which pieces are single-use. A savings claim based on ideal installation conditions may not hold on a roof with substantial variation. Price the complete assembly and its documented work method rather than treating rail-less as automatically cheaper.

sections.title: Asphalt shingles and tile manage water differently
paragraphs: A composition-shingle attachment must integrate with the roof's water-shedding layers. A tile-roof solution may use hooks, replacement pieces or another approved approach, but brittle covering and the relationship to underlying waterproofing introduce different details. The tile itself should not be assumed to be the structural support simply because it is the visible surface.

For each option, ask how the roof interface is flashed or sealed and what remains accessible after installation. Collect details that show the intended structural connection, roof-covering treatment and module support. Repairs to old tile, replacement stock and workmanship responsibility can materially affect cost. Avoid adapting a shingle detail to tile by adding sealant. Let the selected product and roofing instructions establish the detail, and resolve conflicts before hardware arrives.

sections.title: Metal roofing needs the actual profile
paragraphs: Standing-seam clamps and exposed-fastener brackets address different interfaces. A seam clamp engages a specific seam geometry; an exposed-fastener attachment follows its own fastening and sealing details. Identifying a roof merely as metal omits information such as panel profile, material, thickness, attachment arrangement and condition.

S-5!'s clamp-to-seam resource explicitly organizes roof identification and tested holding information. Match the actual roof and clamp, including differences between clamp variants, rather than extrapolating from a similar photograph. Continue the structural review into the roof-panel clips and building. A nonpenetrating module attachment can still overload another link in that chain. Also ask how the assembly accommodates roof movement and material compatibility; these are ownership questions as well as installation questions.

sections.title: Bonding is an assembly property
paragraphs: Many modern mounting systems use evaluated clamp or other interfaces to create the required equipment bonding path. That path depends on the specified combination and installation. A metal-to-metal appearance does not prove continuity under the evaluated conditions, and removing a module can alter the path in some systems.

Keep mechanical compatibility and electrical bonding evidence together but distinct. Determine how rails, splices, modules and any separated array sections are connected in the documented design. Ask which hardware may be reused after service and which must be replaced. The Unirac RM10 manual offers a concrete example of maintenance documentation addressing temporary bonding during module removal. It is evidence for that assembly, not a blanket instruction for every rooftop family.

sections.title: Worked example: compare installed scope

workedExample.title: Two hypothetical mounting offers
givens: Both offers support the same reviewed 16-module layout.
Offer A: hardware $1,400, labor $1,600, approved roof-interface work $400.
Offer B: hardware $1,050, labor $1,750, approved roof-interface work $650.
No difference in electrical equipment or roof condition is assumed.
steps: A installed mounting subtotal = $1,400 + $1,600 + $400 = $3,400.
B saves $350 in hardware but adds $400 elsewhere.
Compare replacement procedures and documentary completeness before deciding whether a $50 difference matters.
workedExample.result: The lower hardware price does not produce the lower complete mounting subtotal.
workedExample.discussion: The example makes no general claim about rail or rail-less labor. Actual scope, roof and installer experience determine the quotation; require equivalent approved assemblies before comparing costs.

sections.title: Comparison worksheet
columns: Questions that select the actual product

Exact profile and clamp; roof-panel load path
paragraphs: The families overlap: a metal-roof system can use rails, and a low-slope system can be partly attached. Describe an option through its interfaces instead of forcing it into a single sales label. This also makes the bill of materials easier to review when a supplier proposes a substitution.

sections.title: Mistakes and an explained exercise
paragraphs: Avoid mixing hardware generations, copying a torque number from another product, or accepting a compatibility statement that omits the exact module model. Check whether decorative skirts or critter guards change an approved installation detail. Ask about roof warranties and replacement work before considering the comparison complete.

exercise.question: A supplier says a seam clamp fits because it can be tightened onto the roof profile. Is that enough to select it?
exercise.answer: No. Physical fit needs tested compatibility and a verified load path for the actual roof.
exercise.explanation: A clamp can appear to grip while lacking evaluated holding evidence for that profile. The panel, clips and supporting building must also transmit the array's loads. Fit is a useful screening observation, not the final acceptance criterion.

sections.title: Low slope is not a single roof type
paragraphs: A low-slope roof is a layered assembly: structure, deck, insulation and covering work together to carry loads and manage water. A mounting design must identify that actual assembly rather than assume that a flat-looking surface can support any ballast tray. Record slope, roof height, parapets, drainage, membrane, insulation and proposed array position.

Ballasted systems use added mass and their evaluated aerodynamic arrangement to resist specified demands. Attached systems transfer forces through specified roof connections. Hybrid arrangements combine these approaches. The choice depends on project evidence, roof capacity and the permitted product configuration. Each creates different concentrated reactions and weatherproofing interfaces. This chapter explains how to review those choices; it does not prescribe ballast quantities, anchor spacing or a membrane detail for an unidentified roof.

figures.caption: This pitched-roof example teaches a force path through module, rail and structure. A ballasted low-slope roof uses different interfaces that need their own review.
figures.alt: A pitched-roof section shows a module, clamp, rail, flashed attachment and rafter carrying gravity and uplift.

sections.title: Ballast is an engineered arrangement
paragraphs: Ballast quantity depends on the selected system, array geometry, roof and site conditions. Moving blocks from one bay to another can change local resistance and loading even if total mass remains constant. Perimeter locations can have different demands from interior locations. A copied ballast count from a neighboring building has no reliable meaning without matching the governing assumptions.

Unirac's RM10 guide points users to project-specific loading and ballast calculations. Its system details are not interchangeable with RM10 EVO or another manufacturer's assembly. Confirm the actual product, model and applicable document revision. Record block dimensions and measured or verified mass as required by the design, because the number of blocks alone does not state the load. Treat missing or moved ballast as a configuration issue requiring the documented review process.

sections.title: Average weight can conceal local pressure
paragraphs: The building sees both total added load and the way that load reaches it. A small contact pad can apply concentrated pressure to insulation or other roof layers, while supporting structural members receive load through the deck. Dividing total ballast by the entire building's area can make the average appear reassuringly low without reducing a heavily loaded local region.

Ask the structural reviewer to assess the actual array footprint, support reactions and load combinations. Ask the roofing team about allowable contact conditions, protective pads and membrane compatibility. Roof-layer compression or displacement can affect drainage and support over time. The design should distinguish whole-building capacity, local roof-deck behavior and the covering/insulation interface. A roof that passes one of these questions may still need changes to address another.

sections.title: Wind and sliding depend on assumptions
paragraphs: A manufacturer's design tool usually works within specified limits for building geometry, roof slope, exposure, roof material and array configuration. Those boundaries are part of the result. Unirac's U-Builder assumptions page also identifies cases needing site-specific engineering, including open structures such as carports. A result from an enclosed-building workflow cannot simply be transferred to a canopy.

Capture inputs, software output and any limitations alongside the project drawings. Ask how site conditions were established, especially roof height, wind design inputs and friction or membrane assumptions. An attractive automatic ballast map is only as credible as the entered conditions and applicability. If a parapet, obstruction or row arrangement changes, identify whether the tool must be rerun. Use the locally adopted code edition and designer's approved project assumptions.

sources.label: Unirac · U-Builder product and engineering assumptions (retrieved 2026-10-05)

sections.title: Protect drainage and maintenance access
paragraphs: Modules, supports and ballast must coexist with drains, scuppers and paths for inspection. Existing ponding or uneven surfaces require attention before the array is installed. A layout that prevents a technician from clearing a drain can create an avoidable operating problem. Preserve access to rooftop mechanical equipment as well as to the solar equipment.

Plan temporary construction loading too. Stacking ballast in one convenient delivery spot produces a different local load from its final distributed arrangement. The approved handling plan should account for access, lifting and roof protection. OSHA's US solar guidance identifies fall hazards around roof edges and skylights; a low pitch does not make an unprotected edge harmless. Document the actual access method and responsible site team rather than treating an overhead pathway line as a complete safety plan.

sources.label: OSHA · Solar energy fall hazards (United States)

sections.title: Worked example: identical mass, different pressure

workedExample.title: Illustrative ballast bookkeeping
givens: A fictional array has 800 kg of ballast plus 400 kg of modules and hardware.
Array footprint: 80 m²; roof area: 400 m².
One hypothetical support carries 60 kg over 0.10 m²; ignore load redistribution and all design combinations.
steps: Total mass = 800 + 400 = 1,200 kg.
Average over the array footprint = 1,200 ÷ 80 = 15 kg/m².
Average over the entire roof = 1,200 ÷ 400 = 3 kg/m².
The hypothetical local contact pressure represented as mass per area is 60 ÷ 0.10 = 600 kg/m², approximately 5.9 kPa under standard gravity.
workedExample.result: The same system has very different averages depending on the chosen area; none establishes roof capacity.
workedExample.discussion: The local illustration shows why the footprint and support contact deserve review. The simplified 60 kg assumption is not an actual reaction calculation, permissible insulation pressure or a ballast recommendation.

sections.title: Compare the complete alternatives
rows: Mass, local pressure, sliding and uplift resistance
Ballast position and roof contact inspections
Both sets of interfaces need records
paragraphs: Compare complete installed scope including roof preparation, lifting, protective interfaces, engineering and future roof work. One design may reduce penetrations but increase mass; another may reduce ballast while introducing roof-interface work. State those consequences in the proposal instead of ranking every ballasted installation above or below every attached one.

sections.title: Mistakes that change the evaluated configuration
paragraphs: Do not add arbitrary blocks to cure uncertainty, assume every membrane has the same friction behavior, or interchange roof pads because their size matches. Do not increase tilt or attach decorative elements without checking the system's approved configuration. The assembled aerodynamic shape may be part of its evaluation.

Module replacement is another design event. Dimensions, frame profile and support zones may affect both mounting and bonding. Keep a service record that identifies which clamps or bonding components require replacement after removal. Photographs of completed bays, drainage clearance and ballast placement provide a baseline for later inspection. Routine owner observations can flag displaced parts; corrective work belongs to personnel who can follow the system's documented procedure.

sections.title: Exercise: a software result outside its scope

exercise.question: A ballasted design tool produces a map for an enclosed warehouse. Can its map approve the same array on an open-sided parking canopy?
exercise.answer: No. The building assumptions and wind behavior differ, and the product's applicability must be checked.
exercise.explanation: U-Builder's published assumptions identify open structures as requiring site-specific engineering. A software output does not override its own limitations. The correct next step is a canopy-specific design review, not copying the warehouse ballast quantities.

paragraphs: Save the applicable assumptions with the output. A credible low-slope proposal shows how total load, local interface, drainage and system applicability were resolved together.

ground-and-pole-mounts.outcome: Select a ground or pole mounting concept using geometry, foundation evidence, access, corrosion and service requirements rather than panel count alone.

sections.title: Choose the structure around the site's job
paragraphs: A multi-post ground rack spreads a table across several supports. A pole-mounted table concentrates its forces into a smaller set of supports, often one principal pole. Fixed and adjustable versions add different mechanisms and operating responsibilities. These labels describe concepts; the actual manufacturer determines permissible modules, table dimensions, tilt positions and structural conditions.

Start with the intended use. A remote pump, a small off-grid property and a larger residential array may value access, space and seasonal adjustment differently. Write the useful generation objective, available land, cable route and maintenance capability. A mount that physically holds the desired module count may still be unsuitable because of wind loading, foundation demands, actuator service or an inaccessible adjustment mechanism. Keep the supporting structure and energy objective in the same decision.

figures.caption: Module-table geometry affects shadows and forces. This conceptual view does not size a post or pole.
figures.alt: Tilted module rows show rise and the separation required for one simplified solar position.

sections.title: Follow forces from table to ground
paragraphs: Downward weight, wind uplift and horizontal forces travel through module interfaces, rails or table members, braces, posts and foundations. A high table or large cantilever can create substantial moments even when module mass seems modest. A pole mount's compact visible footprint does not imply a small underground foundation.

A structural design resolves forces using site inputs and approved configurations. Avoid sizing a footing from panel weight or copying a pole diameter from a photograph. The pole, connection, foundation and soil must work together. Record the manufacturer's required materials and details, because nominally similar pipe and tubing may have different properties. When the module format changes, review table dimensions and mechanical compatibility as well as the electrical design.

sections.title: Soil testing establishes the missing interface
paragraphs: The foundation interacts with real ground, which may vary over a small property. Fill, rock, soft layers, groundwater, frost and corrosion can all matter. The foundation designer determines what investigation and acceptance evidence the project needs. An apparently firm surface does not describe the material carrying uplift or lateral loads below it.

For screw foundations, distinguish installation observations from acceptance criteria. Ease of installation, torque or depth may be relevant only within the selected manufacturer's documented method and project design. IronRidge's ground-screw information directs users to the screw manufacturer's installation instructions as well as its own array assembly manual. Use the approved combination and keep the required field records. Moving a foundation to avoid a rock or buried service must be reviewed for its effect on the arrangement.

sources.label: IronRidge · Ground screw compatibility and site limits

sections.title: Tilt adjustment is an operating commitment
paragraphs: An adjustable table can change orientation seasonally, but its available positions and locking method are product-specific. Evaluate how personnel reach and move it, what loads may be present during adjustment, and whether the owner can reliably follow the documented process. A promised production gain depends on the positions actually used.

Compare fixed and adjustable alternatives with the same weather and system model. A mechanical feature adds value when its modeled benefit exceeds its cost and operating burden for the project. Do not assume that following the sun or increasing winter tilt produces a universal percentage gain. Shade, latitude, weather, module configuration and controls all influence the result. For moving systems, include inspection and replacement access for the mechanism, not just space for the module surface.

sections.title: Corrosion, vegetation and cable routing
paragraphs: Ground structures encounter soil contact, moisture and sometimes salt or agricultural exposure. Document the manufacturer's material and corrosion provisions for the actual environment. The cable route must accommodate support, protection, ground clearance and any movement of an adjustable table. A hinge that moves easily can still strain an incorrectly managed conductor.

Lay out maintenance access before selecting the final row density. Consider drainage, erosion, vegetation management and the equipment used on the property. Tall grass can obstruct access and contribute shade; mowing can damage unprotected wiring. Buried routes need a recorded location and applicable design details. Keep the foundation layout and electrical route together so excavation, inspection and future servicing can be coordinated without guessing where equipment or services were installed.

sections.title: Worked example: why a taller table changes the question

workedExample.title: An illustrative horizontal force on two mounting heights
givens: Hypothetical horizontal resultant force: 2.0 kN.
Case A resultant height: 1.0 m above the reference support point.
Case B height: 2.5 m; same force and no other loads.
This statics example omits actual wind coefficients, load combinations and foundation response.
steps: Moment in A = force × height = 2.0 × 1.0 = 2.0 kN·m.
Moment in B = 2.0 × 2.5 = 5.0 kN·m.
B has 2.5 times the moment about this point under the stated assumptions.
Ask the structural designer to evaluate the complete elevated configuration, rather than selecting the foundation from equal panel mass.
workedExample.result: The same simplified force can create a much larger moment when applied higher.
workedExample.discussion: This arithmetic explains a lever arm. It does not predict design wind force, select pole diameter, specify concrete or establish any allowable load. Real support reactions and soil behavior require the project design.

sections.title: Selection worksheet
rows: Approved model, orientation and clamp zones
paragraphs: Use the worksheet to compare configurations that achieve the same goal. A supplier's price for a table alone is not equivalent to a price that includes foundations, excavation, erection and engineering. Keep exclusions visible and ask how weather or ground conditions affect the quotation.

sections.title: Common mistakes and maintenance handover
paragraphs: Do not treat a pole mount as a way to avoid foundation engineering, assume all ground screws are interchangeable, or use a higher adjustment position without reviewing the approved limits. Do not confuse a module's mechanical test load with capacity of the pole and soil assembly.

At handover, save the approved table configuration, foundation map, field acceptance records and photographs of buried work. Include adjustment instructions only for the exact installed product and clarify who is authorized to operate or service it. After erosion, flooding, impact or unusual movement, the appropriate response is inspection and review. Tightening a visibly loose part without identifying why it moved can obscure a developing foundation or connection problem.

sections.title: Exercise: compact footprint versus complete cost

exercise.question: A pole mount occupies less visible ground than a four-post rack. Does that prove it will require less foundation work?
exercise.answer: No. Concentrated forces and moments can require a substantial pole and foundation.
exercise.explanation: Visible footprint does not express the force distribution or soil response. Compare the designed foundation quantities and installation work for each approved configuration. Fewer posts can be useful for access, but they are not a universal cost or capacity advantage.

paragraphs: The best next step is a documented site and configuration review that connects expected energy, support geometry, foundation evidence and maintainable routing.

solar-canopies.outcome: Write a solar-canopy brief that integrates structural design, occupied space, drainage, electrical routes and the actual solar value.

NREL · PV and energy storage O&M best practices, third edition (2018), NREL/TP-7A40-73822

sections.title: A canopy is an occupied-space project
paragraphs: A solar canopy combines an elevated support structure with photovoltaic equipment while preserving a use underneath. That use may be parking, a walkway or another outdoor activity. The project therefore has at least two success measures: useful solar generation and a space that functions properly for its users. A panel layout that produces energy but obstructs vehicles or drains onto a walkway fails the broader brief.

Begin with the existing use and its constraints. Record vehicle routes, required clearance, pedestrian access, accessibility needs, lighting, drainage and buried services. Then identify the solar objective and electrical destination. A canopy may be attractive where roof area is unavailable or shade for parked vehicles has value, but its new structure and foundations must be included in the installed scope. It should not be priced as a roof array with a few extra posts.

sections.title: An open structure needs its own loading review
paragraphs: A canopy does not share all of an enclosed building's wind conditions. Airflow can interact with both sides of an elevated surface, while column positions and cantilevers determine the structural arrangement. Height, spans and local site conditions matter. Counting module mass or borrowing a rooftop mounting rule leaves the major questions unanswered.

Use a canopy system and site-specific structural package appropriate to the actual project. Schletter's SunRide announcement illustrates a commercial canopy approach with project planning and structural documentation; it does not supply a generic foundation design for every site. Unirac's U-Builder assumptions separately flag open structures such as carports for site-specific engineering. Record the locally adopted requirements and the designer's load assumptions, including module and support compatibility, rather than transferring an enclosed-roof software output.

sources.label: Schletter · SunRide carport manufacturer announcement
Unirac · U-Builder product and engineering assumptions (retrieved 2026-10-05)

sections.title: Clearance is three-dimensional
paragraphs: A parking plan must preserve vehicle movement, door opening, pedestrian routes and clearance under the lowest relevant part of the structure. A nominal canopy height may refer to a point that is not the lowest beam, equipment enclosure or cable route. Sloped ground can reduce clearance locally. Record the vehicle envelope and actual finished levels.

Column positions can affect turning and parking even when the bays look generous in plan view. Consider impact exposure and the appropriate protection as part of the project design. Future changes such as taller fleet vehicles or altered parking aisles should be captured in the brief. A canopy that is difficult to use can lose practical value despite excellent energy production. Compare proposed alternatives using drawings that show both solar geometry and the occupied space.

sections.title: Waterproof shelter must be an explicit scope
paragraphs: A row of ordinary framed PV modules is not automatically a continuous waterproof roof. Module gaps, mounting interfaces and penetrations need an approved weather-management arrangement if dry shelter is part of the promise. Ask whether the system includes gutters, seals or another documented method and how that method is maintained.

Show where rainwater discharges and how snow or debris may affect use beneath the canopy. Runoff concentrated at one edge can create a different site problem from the existing open parking area. Drainage should coordinate with finished ground levels and pedestrian routes. Keep solar and shelter warranties distinct, including responsibility for water leaks. If a design provides shade but allows some rainfall through the module gaps, state that clearly in the brief and quotation rather than allowing the word canopy to imply dry parking.

sections.title: Electrical integration and EV charging are separate decisions
paragraphs: Generation may serve nearby loads, storage or permitted grid export depending on the electrical architecture and utility agreement. An EV charger beneath the canopy is a separate load with its own capacity and operating schedule. Solar nameplate power does not prove that vehicles can charge at their full rating at every moment.

Draw a conceptual boundary map showing PV, conversion equipment, optional storage, chargers and the building or utility interface. Ask how cable routes are protected from weather, impact and maintenance activity. Controls may coordinate charging with available solar or site demand, but the actual supported behavior needs documentation. A midday generation surplus and evening vehicle charging are different time patterns; an annual energy balance alone cannot establish that the canopy continuously powers all charging without grid imports.

figures.caption: Generic DC and AC coupling paths help define a canopy's electrical integration. This is not a canopy construction or wiring drawing.
figures.alt: PV connects either to a DC bus with storage or through a PV inverter into an AC bus with separate battery conversion.

sections.title: Worked example: daily solar and vehicle energy

workedExample.title: A fictional workplace canopy
givens: PV system: 20 kW DC; assumed daily equivalent full-power hours: 4.
Assumed aggregate energy factor: 0.80 after modeled losses.
Four vehicles each need 12 kWh that day; no storage is included.
This is a daily energy screen, not a charger power or service-capacity design.
steps: Estimated daily AC solar energy = 20 × 4 × 0.80 = 64 kWh.
Vehicle energy request = 4 × 12 = 48 kWh.
Daily energy surplus before other site loads = 64 − 48 = 16 kWh.
Review arrival times, charge rates, solar profile and other site loads to determine actual simultaneous imports or curtailment.
workedExample.result: The assumed daily solar energy exceeds vehicle demand, but timing and power limits remain unresolved.
workedExample.discussion: Four 7 kW chargers would request 28 kW if operating together, which exceeds the 20 kW DC nameplate even before conversion and weather effects. Energy sufficiency over a day is not a guarantee of instantaneous charger supply.

sections.title: Compare solar and non-solar scope
paragraphs: Keep the cost of the new canopy structure visible. If shade or shelter has value, assess it explicitly instead of forcing all value into electricity savings. This creates a more honest comparison with roof or ground alternatives.

sections.title: Mistakes and long-term access
paragraphs: Avoid calculating payback from panel cost alone, assuming every module is approved for overhead occupancy, or accepting a waterproof promise without the corresponding assembly details. Do not let charging equipment or decorative additions create unreviewed wind, clearance or routing changes.

Plan how modules, drainage components and lighting are inspected or replaced above an active parking area. Service may require temporary closures and suitable access equipment. A contract should explain responsibility for these arrangements. Keep photographs and serial records where a future operator can find them. An attractive opening-day canopy remains an asset only if its structure, occupied space and electrical equipment can be maintained without improvising access over vehicles and pedestrians.

sections.title: Exercise: energy versus simultaneous demand

exercise.question: The example produces 64 kWh per day. Can four vehicles therefore always charge at 7 kW each directly from the canopy?
exercise.answer: No. Their combined 28 kW demand and charging times must be compared with actual available AC solar power.
exercise.explanation: Daily kWh integrate power over time. A daily energy surplus can coexist with imports during charging and export or curtailment at another time. Chargers, controls, storage and utility capacity determine the supported operation.

paragraphs: Finish the brief with both the solar success measure and the occupied-space requirements. The quotation can then describe a complete canopy project rather than an isolated module purchase.

commissioning.outcome: Prepare subsystem commissioning gates, acceptance evidence and owner handover records while reserving electrical tests and energization for qualified personnel using the exact manuals.

sections.title: Commissioning proves a defined configuration
paragraphs: Commissioning checks whether the installed system corresponds to its design and performs the required functions. It is not simply the first moment an inverter displays power. Define the configuration, operating modes and acceptance criteria before the test day. A grid-connected array, a battery backup system and an off-grid system require different evidence because their intended functions differ.

Use subsystem gates. Records and mechanical completion precede electrical verification; verified configuration precedes controlled energization; operating checks precede handover. Each gate has an expected result, an accountable person and a record. This chapter teaches how to prepare and interpret that process. It is not a live-testing, switching or energization procedure. Qualified personnel must use the exact installed equipment manuals, approved design and applicable jurisdictional requirements.

figures.caption: Commissioning gates proceed from records and inspection to controlled functional validation and a saved baseline. The diagram contains no switching sequence.
figures.alt: A staged flow shows documentation, mechanical review, electrical verification, functional tests and handover.

sections.title: Freeze the design and reconcile the installation
paragraphs: Collect current drawings, approved equipment lists, manufacturer manuals, protection settings, firmware requirements and inspection status. Reconcile serial numbers and installed models with those documents. A substituted module, battery or transfer device should trigger review before tests begin; otherwise the team may be validating a configuration that was never designed.

Keep an as-built string and circuit map. Record labels, conductor identities, module allocation, battery configuration and communications connections. Document work hidden behind modules or covers, including the relevant assembly and torque records. Missing paperwork is not just administrative inconvenience: it can prevent interpreting a measurement or tracing an alarm. Resolve conflicting design revisions so every participant knows which expected values and operating modes apply.

sections.title: Mechanical and environmental readiness
paragraphs: Inspect the installation against the selected manuals and approved drawings. This includes support, access, cable management, enclosure suitability, barriers, equipment clearances and environmental conditions. Confirm the roof or foundation work has reached its required acceptance point. Protect the working area from unrelated activity during commissioning.

Battery and inverter placement can affect airflow, temperatures and service access. A neat equipment wall does not establish correct clearances or compatible enclosures. Verify the physical installation before interpreting software status as readiness. If a component is missing, damaged or improperly supported, record it and stop the dependent tests. Commissioning should expose unresolved installation issues rather than create a persuasive screenshot while the physical configuration remains incomplete.

sections.title: Electrical verification needs a planned safety boundary
paragraphs: PV can generate DC whenever illuminated, batteries store energy, and utility or generator sources may remain available elsewhere in the system. A front-panel off state does not establish safe isolation of every source. OSHA's US electrical and lockout/tagout resources identify the need to control electrical hazards and all relevant energy sources during service. The project team determines the applicable work procedures and authorized personnel.

The test plan identifies which verification activities apply to the installed equipment and how they can be performed without damaging it. Continuity, polarity, insulation and other checks are not interchangeable. Some equipment must be disconnected or handled differently for particular tests. Record instruments, method, conditions and results under the qualified team's procedure. Do not improvise a high-voltage insulation test across connected electronics because a generic checklist includes the words insulation resistance.

sources.label: OSHA · Solar energy lockout/tagout (United States)
OSHA · Solar energy electrical hazards (United States)

sections.title: Startup order is product-specific
paragraphs: Some battery charge controllers depend on seeing the battery before PV for automatic voltage recognition. Victron's SmartSolar MPPT 150/60–250/70 installation documentation specifies its connection process and exceptions. That is evidence for those models, not a universal solar startup recipe. Proprietary storage, hybrid conversion and grid-interactive systems can have different requirements.

Commissioning may also require installer training, supported devices and the manufacturer's application workflow. Enphase's November 2024 US off-grid technical brief lists specific prerequisite devices and training for that architecture. Use the correct regional guide and firmware requirements. At each permitted stage, compare actual state with the expected result and documented stop criteria. Unexpected readings, alarms, odor, heating or physical damage call for stopping through the site's safe procedure and resolving the cause before progression.

Enphase · Commissioning an off-grid system, TEB-00203-1.0-EN (November 2024, US)

sections.title: Worked example: an acceptance result with conditions

workedExample.title: Interpreting a fictional low-load power check
givens: A controlled test uses a known 1.0 kW AC load for 15 minutes.
Metered AC energy during the interval: 0.247 kWh.
Test plan allows a ±5% interval-energy tolerance for this particular calibrated setup.
The example says nothing about safe connection, protection or switching.
steps: Expected energy = 1.0 kW × 0.25 h = 0.250 kWh.
Relative difference = −0.003 ÷ 0.250 × 100 = −1.2%.
Record the load, measurement boundary, interval, meter and conditions; classify this one check as within the assumed tolerance.
workedExample.result: The interval-energy result passes the fictional criterion; it does not establish every backup function.
workedExample.discussion: Surge starting, phase balance, transfer, depletion recovery and charging are separate functions. The ±5% value is invented for this example and must not be treated as a universal commissioning standard.

sections.title: Functional validation follows the project brief
rows: Power and energy at stated conditions
Do designated loads and isolation work?
Can the owner operate and report issues?
paragraphs: An outage test must follow the manufacturer-approved method and authorized site procedure. Do not create an outage by improvised connections or unsafe switching. Identify which functions are demonstrated and which remain deferred, with the conditions required to complete them.

sections.title: Save a baseline and close the handover
paragraphs: Record operating conditions with measurements. Solar power without irradiance, temperature and system state is difficult to compare later. Battery state, available charge acceptance and export limits can explain production restrictions. Keep firmware, settings, alarms, meter directions and the completed test record alongside photographs and final drawings.

Give the owner documented operating controls, emergency information, service contacts, warranties and monitoring access. Confirm that required inspection and utility permission have been obtained before the relevant operation. A technically functioning installation and authorization to export are separate matters. Handover should list accepted functions, unresolved items and responsibilities. Do not mark an unperformed recovery or backup test as passed simply because normal grid-connected production looks reasonable.

sections.title: Mistakes and an explained exercise
paragraphs: Avoid universal power-on sequences, changing several settings at once, undocumented firmware updates during diagnosis, and accepting a green communications icon as proof of electrical function. Keep commissioning evidence tied to the exact installed configuration so later changes can be reviewed.

exercise.question: The app reports all devices online and solar output is visible. Does that prove the selected backup circuits work during an outage?
exercise.answer: No. Communications and normal production are only part of commissioning.
exercise.explanation: Backup needs the documented isolation, transfer, supported-load and recovery behavior. Its approved functional validation is separate from a network-status check and should appear explicitly in the acceptance record.

troubleshooting.outcome: Organize safe observations, separate energy-flow and monitoring faults, and produce a reproducible service report instead of changing settings blindly.
